title: Attention and Transformers
tagline: Every token looks at every token
summary: Attention as a soft dictionary lookup, scaled dot-product attention with masks, multi-head attention with its reshapes, positional encoding, and the full Transformer block, all as needed for the 2026 Final Task 3.
syllabus: IOAI 2B5 Transformers (theory for text and image)
NOAI 2026 Final Task 3: scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding
Causal masks, cross-attention, O(n²) complexity, LayerNorm and residuals

lessons.title: Attention as a soft lookup
lessons.summary: Queries, keys and values: matching a question against labels to blend the answers.
objectives: You can describe the roles of query, key and value
You can compute attention weights with softmax over similarities
You can explain how attention builds context-dependent word representations

concepts.name: A soft dictionary lookup
concepts.explain: A normal dictionary returns the value whose key exactly matches your query. Attention compares the query with every key (by dot product), turns the scores into weights with softmax, and returns a weighted average of all the values. Close matches dominate, but everything contributes a little.
concepts.analogy: Asking a group chat 'who knows a good chicken rice stall?': replies from friends whose interests match your question count most, and you blend their suggestions.

visual.shows: A draggable 2D query arrow, four key arrows with attached value colours, the similarity scores, softmax weight bars and the blended output colour.
visual.interaction: Drag the query; scale it up to make the softmax sharper; edit keys and values.
visual.aha: Attention is a differentiable, weighted lookup instead of an exact match.

concepts.name: Words attending to words
concepts.explain: In self-attention every word produces a query, key and value. A word like 'it' in 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired' attends strongly to 'animal', so its new representation includes that meaning. Each word's output is a context-dependent mix of the whole sentence.
concepts.analogy: In a group project, each member updates their understanding by listening most to the teammates most relevant to their part.

visual.shows: A sentence with arcs from a selected word to every other word, arc thickness showing illustrative attention weights, and a bar chart of the weights.
visual.interaction: Click any word to see its attention; switch the ending word (tired/wide) and see 'it' shift its focus between 'animal' and 'street'.
visual.aha: Attention lets the same word mean different things in different contexts.

checkpoint_focus: Output is weighted average of values

lessons.title: Scaled dot-product attention and masks
lessons.summary: The formula softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V step by step with shapes, why we divide by √d_k, and padding and causal masks.
objectives: You can compute attention for a tiny Q, K, V by hand
You can state the shapes of QKᵀ and the output
You can build causal and padding masks and apply them with −∞ before softmax

concepts.name: The attention matrix step by step
concepts.explain: Stack the queries as rows of Q and keys as rows of K. QKᵀ is a T×T table of every query-key score; dividing by √d_k and applying softmax across each row gives attention weights; multiplying by V mixes the value vectors. For a batch, shapes are (B, T, d) → scores (B, T, T) → output (B, T, d_v).
concepts.analogy: A seating chart where every student rates every other student's relevance, then each student writes notes mixing what the highly-rated ones said.

visual.shows: Small Q, K and V MatrixGrids (3 tokens, d = 2) with integer values; steps compute QKᵀ, scale, softmax per row, then multiply by V, with shapes annotated at each step.
visual.interaction: Step forward and back; edit Q, K, V values; hover a weight to see which query and key it links.
visual.aha: Attention is two matrix multiplications with a row-wise softmax in between.

concepts.name: Why divide by √d_k
concepts.explain: If query and key components have variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k, so scores grow with dimension. Large scores push softmax into a near one-hot output with tiny gradients. Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores' variance at about 1.
concepts.analogy: Grading on a curve: without rescaling, a longer exam produces bigger score gaps, making the ranking all-or-nothing.

visual.shows: A histogram of dot-product scores for random vectors of dimension d_k, and the resulting softmax weights for one row, with and without scaling.
visual.interaction: Slide d_k from 2 to 512; toggle scaling on and off.
visual.aha: Without scaling, high-dimensional attention saturates and stops learning.

concepts.name: Causal and padding masks
concepts.explain: A mask sets forbidden scores to −∞ before softmax so their weights become exactly 0. A causal (look-ahead) mask blocks each position from seeing future positions, required for next-token prediction; torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T), diagonal=1) marks the future positions. A padding mask blocks attention to [PAD] tokens.
concepts.analogy: Covering the answers further down the page while you work through a worksheet.

visual.shows: The T×T score grid with masked cells shaded, the row-wise softmax weights after masking, and the PyTorch mask expression and its boolean grid.
visual.interaction: Toggle causal and padding masks; change T and padding length; switch between triu/tril and the 'True means keep' vs 'True means mask' conventions.
visual.aha: Masking is just −∞ in the right cells, but mixing up mask conventions is a classic bug.

lessons.title: Multi-head attention
lessons.summary: Running several attention heads in parallel on slices of the embedding, the view/transpose reshapes, concatenation and output projection.
objectives: You can compute head_dim = d_model / num_heads
You can trace the shape changes (B, T, d) → (B, h, T, d/h) and back
You can explain why multiple heads help
You can count the parameters of a multi-head attention layer

concepts.name: Splitting into heads
concepts.explain: Multi-head attention projects the input into queries, keys and values, then splits the d_model features into h heads of size d_model/h. In PyTorch: reshape (B, T, d) to (B, T, h, d/h), transpose to (B, h, T, d/h), run attention per head, transpose back and merge to (B, T, d), then apply an output projection W_O.
concepts.analogy: A committee splitting a report into sections so each member reviews one aspect in parallel, then merging their notes.

visual.shows: A (T, d_model) block sliced into coloured head bands, rearranged into h separate (T, d/h) blocks, processed and then re-merged, with code lines highlighted for each reshape.
visual.interaction: Slide d_model and number of heads (with a warning when d_model is not divisible); play the reshapes; step through code.
visual.aha: Multi-head attention is the same attention run on slices, held together by careful reshapes.

concepts.name: Different heads, different relationships
concepts.explain: Each head has its own projections, so different heads can specialise: one might track the previous word, another subject-verb links, another punctuation. Concatenating them gives a richer representation than one big head with the same total size.
concepts.analogy: A panel of judges at a cooking contest, each focusing on taste, presentation or originality.

visual.shows: Attention-weight heat maps for four illustrative heads on the same sentence, each showing a distinct pattern (previous token, same word, subject-verb, start token).
visual.interaction: Click a head to enlarge its map; hover cells to see token pairs.
visual.aha: Several smaller heads capture several kinds of relationship at once.

checkpoint_focus: Linear projections W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O

lessons.title: Positional encoding and the Transformer block
lessons.summary: Why attention needs position information, sinusoidal and learned encodings, and how attention, feed-forward layers, residuals and LayerNorm form a block.
objectives: You can explain why self-attention is permutation-invariant without positions
You can compute sinusoidal positional encoding values
You can describe a Transformer block and encoder vs decoder blocks
You can explain O(n²) cost in sequence length

concepts.name: Attention ignores order without positions
concepts.explain: Self-attention treats its input as a set: shuffle the words and each word's output is just shuffled the same way, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look alike. Adding a positional encoding vector to each token embedding gives the model word-order information.
concepts.analogy: A pile of numbered exam scripts dropped on the floor: without the numbers, you cannot tell the order.

visual.shows: A sentence, its attention outputs, and the same for a shuffled sentence; without positional encoding the outputs are a permutation of each other, with it they genuinely differ.
visual.interaction: Shuffle the words; toggle positional encoding.
visual.aha: Order information must be injected explicitly into a Transformer.

concepts.name: Sinusoidal positional encoding
concepts.explain: The original Transformer uses sine and cosine waves of different frequencies: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d)). Low dimensions oscillate quickly and high dimensions slowly, so every position gets a unique pattern, and nearby positions get similar ones. Many models instead learn position embeddings.
concepts.analogy: A clock with second, minute and hour hands: together they give every moment a unique reading.

visual.shows: A heat map of PE values (positions down, dimensions across), a plot of a few dimensions as waves, and a similarity matrix between positions.
visual.interaction: Slide d_model and sequence length; click a cell to see its exact sin/cos computation; introduce a 'bug' (e.g. wrong exponent) and compare heat maps.
visual.aha: Each dimension is a wave of a different frequency, and the combination works like a timestamp.

concepts.name: The Transformer block
concepts.explain: A block applies multi-head self-attention, adds the input back (residual) and normalises (LayerNorm), then applies a small feed-forward network to each token, again with a residual and LayerNorm. Encoders stack these blocks; decoders add causal masking and a cross-attention layer that attends to the encoder's outputs.
concepts.analogy: A study group round: discuss with everyone (attention), keep your original notes (residual), tidy up (norm), then think alone (feed-forward).

visual.shows: A block diagram with tensor shapes on each arrow; stepping highlights each sub-layer; an encoder/decoder toggle adds the masked attention and cross-attention layers.
visual.interaction: Step through; toggle encoder or decoder; set the number of blocks to stack.
visual.aha: A Transformer is a stack of identical blocks, each mixing tokens (attention) then processing them individually (FFN).

concepts.name: Quadratic cost
concepts.explain: Self-attention computes a score for every pair of tokens, so memory and time grow with T², the square of the sequence length. Doubling the context length quadruples the attention cost, which is the main challenge for long-context models.
concepts.analogy: A class where every student must shake hands with every other student: double the class size, four times the handshakes.

visual.shows: A T×T grid that grows as T increases, with a plot of attention memory against T on linear and log axes.
visual.interaction: Slide T from 16 to 8192; compare with a linear-cost curve.
visual.aha: Attention's pairwise table is why long contexts are expensive.
